topics.label: Introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture within the cancer course and states what students should learn about cancer causation.

topics.label: Mutation, clonal evolution and cancer susceptibility
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics establish how mutations can give rise to cancer through clonal selection within a susceptible cell and a permissive microenvironment.

topics.label: Environmental cancer risks and the bad luck debate
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how far cancer risk can be attributed to environmental exposure rather than unavoidable processes or inherited susceptibility.

topics.label: Infectious causes of cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infections contribute to carcinogenesis, using Burkitt lymphoma as a detailed example of interacting infectious factors.

topics.label: Mechanisms of environmentally induced DNA damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how environmental exposures produce DNA damage and mutations, with their effects shaped by cellular metabolism and repair.

topics.label: Tumour initiation and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics distinguish mutation-producing initiation from the promotion that enables initiated cells to proliferate into tumours.

topics.label: Tissue and developmental specificity of carcinogenesis
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics complete and recap the account of carcinogenic mechanisms by emphasising how the exposed tissue and its developmental state affect susceptibility.

topics.label: Methods for investigating carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine the evidence and limitations of methods used to connect exposures with mutations and cancer development.

topics.label: Closing summary and risk–benefit decisions
topics.groupedBecause: This closing draws together the lecture’s conclusions and frames everyday exposure decisions as a balance of risks and benefits.
